lesson.title: Tipping Point: How a Neuron Decides Whether to Fire
lesson.summary: Synaptic threshold refers to the minimum level of depolarization a neuron's membrane must reach, generally through the combined effect of many synaptic inputs, before it will fire an all-or-none action potential.
lesson.body:
A single neuron typically receives input from thousands of synapses across its dendrites and cell body at any given moment, some of that input excitatory and pushing it toward firing, some inhibitory and pushing it away. Whether the neuron actually fires an action potential comes down to a single question: does the combined effect of all that input reach threshold at the axon hillock.

Threshold is usually around negative 55 millivolts, a step up from the resting potential of about negative 70 millivolts covered earlier. Excitatory postsynaptic potentials, EPSPs, are small, graded depolarizations that nudge the membrane potential upward, closer to negative 55, typically produced by ligand-gated channels letting Na+ into the cell. Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials, IPSPs, do the opposite, either hyperpolarizing the membrane further below rest or otherwise holding it away from threshold, typically by letting Cl- in or K+ out. On their own, a single EPSP or IPSP is rarely large enough to decide the outcome, which is exactly why the neuron needs a way to combine many of them.

What actually pushes a neuron to threshold is summation. In temporal summation, EPSPs arriving in rapid succession from the same synapse add together before the earlier ones have faded, building toward threshold. In spatial summation, EPSPs arriving simultaneously from many different synapses across the dendrites combine their effects at once. The axon hillock functions as the neuron's integration point, continuously tallying the net balance of every excitatory and inhibitory signal arriving at that moment.

This connects directly to the all-or-none principle: the summation process leading up to threshold is graded, EPSPs and IPSPs vary continuously in size and can partially cancel each other, but the outcome once threshold is reached or not reached is strictly binary. Either the sum crosses threshold and a full, uniform action potential fires, or it falls short and nothing happens at all. Threshold functions like a gate converting continuously varying, analog input into a discrete, all-or-nothing output, the same all-or-none logic that governs the action potential itself once threshold is actually crossed.

A useful way to picture this is a group of people separately murmuring warnings, no single voice is loud enough to make someone jump, but if enough voices overlap and say "watch out" at once, the combined volume crosses a threshold and triggers an immediate reaction, while a lone reassuring voice mixed in might cancel out part of that effect. This threshold logic is what lets a neuron filter out random background noise and respond only to genuinely strong or converging signals, the same filtering that, at the network level, lets sensory information rise to conscious attention only when it truly matters.
